This R script identifies differentially expressed genes between esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) tissue and paired normal tissue from six individual patients. MultiQC analysis was performed using an HPC environment, and this script processes pre-aligned gene count data published on GEO. The analysis begins with general data exploration, followed by preprocessing, normalization, and statistical analysis using the "edgeR" package.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## General info
- Species: Homo Sapiens
- Sequencing device: Illumina HiSeq 2500
- Single- or paired-end sequencing: Paired-end sequencing
- Samples: This dataset includes six ESCC tumor and six adjacent normal tissue samples obtained from six individuals
- Muli Qc performed with HPC. Trimming and mapping has not been done due to the issue regarding the access into HPC. Instead, statistical analysis performed with raw count data downloaded from NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE194116).


### Load dataset
```{r}
# Read in text file 
rnadatafull <- read.table("GSE194116_Raw_gene_counts_matrix.txt", header = T, sep = "\t", quote = "")

#Have a look at the data
head(rnadatafull)
```
```{r}
# save ensemble IDs and gene names in separate variable
geneIDs <- rnadatafull[,1:2]

head(geneIDs)
```


## 1. Preprocess data
```{r}
## Separate numerical data (count data) from annotation
rownames(rnadatafull) <- 1:nrow(rnadatafull) 
rnadata <- rnadatafull[, 3:14]

## Make annotation for design later on
individuals <- factor(c("patient1", "patient2", "patient3", "patient4", "patient5", "patient6","patient1", "patient2", "patient3", "patient4", "patient5", "patient6"))

cvst <- factor(c("Normal", "Normal", "Normal", "Normal", "Normal", "Normal","ESCC","ESCC","ESCC","ESCC","ESCC","ESCC"))
```

### 1.1. Further preprocessing
```{r}
# Create DGEList object: 'rnadata' contains the count data, and 'rnadatafull[, 1:2]' contains gene information 
y <- DGEList(rnadata, genes = rnadatafull[, 1:2])

# Optional filter
# 'lib.size' refers to the library size of each sample. We calculate CPM (Counts Per Million) values,and apply a filtering threshold (cutoff) to remove genes with low counts.
cutoff <- 3 / (mean(y$samples$lib.size) / 1000000) 

#Keep genes with CPM greater than the cutoff in at least 6 samples:
keep <- rowSums(cpm(y) > cutoff) >= 6
#This provides information on how many genes passed the filtering criteria
summary(keep)

# Update DGEList object to include only the filtered genes
y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] 

```

### 1.2. Normalization
```{r}
y <- calcNormFactors(y)

# Have a look at the library sizes and normalization factors
y$samples
```

### 1.3. MDS plot
- Visualize Sample Similarity
-The MDS plot clearly distinguishes between the Normal and ECA groups, effectively highlighting significant biological differences between the two conditions. The variability within the ECA group suggests heterogeneity, offering potential insights through further analysis.
```{r}
# Define colors for Normal (black) and ECA (red)
colors <- ifelse(grepl("^Normal", rownames(y$samples)), "black", "red")

# Plot MDS with specified colors
plotMDS(y, col=colors, main = "MDS Plot: Normal vs ECA")

# Add legend
legend("topright", legend=c("Normal", "ECA"), col=c("black", "red"), pch=16)

```


## 2. EdgeR differential expression analysis - Paired analysis 
- as my dataset has been obtained from paired design experiment, perform paired analysis

### 2.1. Create design matrix
In paired data analysis, I need to account for within-individual variation to correctly identify the effects of the variable of interest (cvst in this case). The design matrix (model.matrix) is created to include both the condition (cvst) and the individual effect (individuals) as factors. This ensures that any differences detected between conditions are not confounded by differences inherent to the individuals.

```{r}
# Create a design matrix: The 'cvst' variable represents the condition (e.g., Normal vs ECA), and 'individuals' represents the paired samples (e.g., patient1, patient2, etc.).

# The design matrix specifies how the data is modeled in terms of the experimental design.
design <- model.matrix(~ cvst + individuals)
design
rownames(design) <- colnames(y)
y <- estimateDisp(y, design) 
```

### 2.2  Plot BCV (biological coefficient of variation) plot
- shows the relationship between the biological variation of gene expression
- The graph shows high variability in lowly expressed genes, with variability decreasing and stabilizing as expression levels increase. The blue trend line effectively captures the decreasing variability pattern, and most genes are close to the red common BCV line, indicating that dispersion estimates are appropriately calculated. Highly variable genes may require further analysis.
```{r}
plotBCV(y, main = "BCV Plot: Biological Coefficient of Variation")
```

### 2.3. Fitting model and making a qq-plot to evaluate goodness of fit.
-The central points follow the theoretical distribution well, indicating the model fits most of the data appropriately. However, deviations at the tails suggest the model may not handle extreme values effectively. 
```{r}
# glmQLFit, glmLRT 수행
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design)
gof(fit,plot=TRUE)
```

### 2.4. glmQSFTest
- Evaluate the significance of coefficients (in this case, the second coefficient).The argument `coef = 2` specifies that the second coefficient in the model. The null hypothesis tested here is that there is no difference in expression between the groups being compared (e.g., Normal vs. ESCC).
```{r}
# glmQLFTest() performs a Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) based on the fitted model
qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = 2)
summary(qlf)

resP <- topTags(qlf, n = nrow(qlf$table))
# Save the full result of the differential expression analysis to a text file
write.table(resP$table , file = "resP_edgeR_ESCC.txt", col.names = T, row.names = F, sep = "\t", quote = F)

rownames(resP$table) <- y$genes$ensembl_id
# Filter the result to only include genes with a p-value less than 0.05 (statistically significant genes)
resP_edgeR <- resP$table[resP$table[, ncol(resP$table)] < 0.05, ]

# Display the number of rows (genes) in the filtered result
num_rows <- nrow(resP_edgeR)
cat("Number of rows in resP_edgeR:", num_rows, "\n")

dim(resP_edgeR)
down_regulated <- sum(resP_edgeR$logFC < 0)
down_regulated
up_regulated <- sum(resP_edgeR$logFC > 0)
up_regulated
```

### 2.5. Create Volvano plot
- visualize the results of differential expression analysis
- Genes on the left and right are downregulated and upregulated, respectively. Black points represent genes with no significant change.
```{r}
# -log10 transform of Pvalue
resP$table$negLogP <- -log10(resP$table$PValue)

with(resP$table, plot(logFC, negLogP, 
                      pch = 16, cex = 0.6, 
                      col = ifelse(PValue < 0.05, "red", "black"), 
                      main = "Volcano Plot: Differential Expression", 
                      xlab = "Log2 Fold Change", 
                      ylab = "-Log10 P-value"))

abline(h = -log10(0.05), col = "blue")
```

### 2.6. Creating MA plot
-Visualize the relationship between the mean expression level (average expression) and the log fold change (difference in expression) for each gene between two conditions.
-The red points, which are spread out, indicate genes with significant differences in expression between the tumor and normal tissue samples. These are the genes that are most likely biologically relevant for further investigation.
```{r}
with(resP$table , plot(logCPM , logFC , pch = 16, cex = 0.2, main = "MA-plot of log fold changes between expression values in tumor and normal tissue."))
with(resP$table, points(logCPM[FDR < 0.05], logFC[FDR < 0.05], pch =
                          16, col = "red", cex = 0.6)) 
 
```

### 2.7 Plot histogram of P-values
- visualize the distribution of p-values obtained from statistical tests, to evaluate the reliability of the results.
- The majority of p-values are very small, indicating strong evidence for the effects tested in most of the comparisons.
```{r}
hist(resP$table$PValue, main = "Histogram of P-values", xlab = "P-value", col = "lightblue")

```

### 2.8. Top10 differentially expressed genes
- Display the most significant differential expression results (top10) between normal and ESCC tissue in the RNA-seq analysis.
```{r}
head(resP$table[, c(1, 2, 3, 6, 7)], 10)
```
## 3. Gene Set Analysis
```{r}
# Display the first 10 rows of resP_edgeR
head(resP_edgeR, 10)

EntrezIDs <- mapIds(org.Hs.eg.db, rownames(resP_edgeR), 'ENTREZID', 'ENSEMBL')
sign_genes_entrez <- resP_edgeR[!(duplicated(EntrezIDs) | is.na(EntrezIDs)), ]
rownames(sign_genes_entrez) <- EntrezIDs[!(duplicated(EntrezIDs) | is.na(EntrezIDs))]

goanaOut <- goana(de=rownames(sign_genes_entrez), species="Hs", trend=T)
goanaOut <- goanaOut[order(goanaOut$P.DE, decreasing=FALSE),] 
goanaOut$FDR.DE <- p.adjust(goanaOut$P.DE, method="BH")
topGORNA <- topGO(goanaOut, ontology="BP", number=50) 

goanaOut_BP <- goanaOut[goanaOut$Ont == "BP",] 
print(paste("Amount of significant GO Biological Process terms:",
as.character(sum(goanaOut_BP$FDR.DE < 0.05))))
topGORNA[order(topGORNA$N),]
#### Gene Set Analysis
# GO analysis (Biological Process)

go_results <- enrichGO(gene = rownames(sign_genes_entrez),
                       OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db,
                       ont = "BP",       # GO Biological Process (BP)
                       pAdjustMethod = "BH",
                       pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
                       qvalueCutoff = 0.05)

go_results_df <- as.data.frame(go_results)
```


```{r}
#visualize only top10 Go results
barplot(go_results, showCategory = 10)

RNAseq_GSA_res <- topGO(goanaOut, ontology="BP", number=100) 

# write GSA results into text file for further analysis
write.table(RNAseq_GSA_res, sep= "\t", file="RNAseq_GSA_results.txt")
```
